newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutor bows to furor, stays on Whitewater probe.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutor bows to furor, stays on Whitewater probe.

text.p: Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr announced on Friday he would remain in charge of an investigation involving President and Mrs. Clinton, vowing to pursue "the truth" and any resultant prosecutions for as long as it takes.

Bowing to nearly a week of public furore and some biting personal criticism of his plan to move to a better career opportunity, Starr abruptly changed course and said he was putting that plan on hold indefinitely.

"I have informed Pepperdine University that I intend to continue as independent counsel, and will assume no duties or responsibilities as dean at Pepperdine until the investigation and any resulting prosecutions of persons named in the order appointing me as independent counsel or high-level government officials have been substantially completed," Starr said in a statement he read out at the independent prosecutor's office.

The "persons named in the order" appointing him were President Bill Clinton, Hillary Rodham Clinton and James McDougal, their business partner in the Whitewater land deal and head of a failed Arkansas Savings and Loan. McDougal has been convicted on bank fraud charges and Starr's office is reportedly seeking his cooperation as a witness.
"My commitment is to the American people and to the pursuit of the truth, and I will seek to fulfil that commitment to the best of my ability and for as long as it takes," Starr said.
He expressed regret his decision to shift jobs "may have called that commitment into question."

Pepperdine University, located in Malibu, California, announced on Monday Starr had accepted the appointment to become dean of its law school and was expected to leave the special prosecutor post for his new duties by August.

His decision to walk away from the highest-profile investigative job in the United States, and one possibly involving the fate of the president and his wife, created a sensation -- and Washington was soon awash in speculation as to what it might mean.

The predominant conclusion of legal experts and political analysts -- despite Starr's protestations -- was that the move suggested he was leaving because he had not amassed enough evidence to make a prosecutable case against the Clintons. The conclusion was, they must be home free.
In trying to counter that guesswork, Starr insisted he move meant nothing more than that he was accepting a fine career opportunity and a stroke of good fortune for himself and his family.

"It is wrong, indeed it is dangerous, to draw any conclusions based on my personal situation," he said in a speech on Wednesday, insisting that the investigation was far from over but would be pursued by capable assistants instead of himself.

Even so, White House aides could barely conceal their glee at his initial decision to leave. Clinton had long ago endorsed the view that Starr, a Republican, was running a politically inspired investigation. The president is a Democrat.
The White House staff mood darkened considerably when Friday's news of Starr's reversal broke. They declined any comment beyond personal puzzlement at his on-again, off-again moves.

Starr's inquiry started in 1994 as a probe of the Whitewater land deal involving the Clintons when the president was governor of Arkansas as well as the failure of an Arkansas savings and loan institution run by McDougal.
It has since expanded to include a number of White House controversies including the firing of the travel office staff and the obtaining of FBI personal files.
